title: Follow the Encounter Trail
imageAlt: Selected sequence: Homonhon landfall on 17 March 1521, Limasawa later in March, Cebu arrival on 7 April. Arrows show order, not distance.
content:
Your mission is to build an encounter report. An encounter is a meeting between people. The expedition met communities with their own leaders, knowledge and connections. Their history did not begin when the ships arrived.

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) marker records landfall at Homonhon on 17 March 1521. Landfall means reaching land after travelling by sea. Do not confuse it with an earlier sighting from a ship. The expedition later visited Limasawa, then reached Cebu on 7 April. This is a selected sequence, not every stop.

Watch how: find a place and its event, compare its position with the other cards, then explain the order. A landing at Homonhon happened before the visit to Cebu. This does not show that one place was more important.

The diagram gives event order, not sailing directions or distances. Use the clues to correct a mixed-up report.
clues: Landing is an event
The NHCP Homonhon marker dates landfall to 17 March 1521. Seeing land and stepping ashore are different events.
Follow the sequence
For these selected stops, read Homonhon before Limasawa before Cebu. Other stops are omitted.
Limit the claim
Visiting three places does not mean gaining control of every island or meeting every community.
task: Which report follows the selected encounter sequence?
Homonhon, then Limasawa, then Cebu
Cebu, then Homonhon, then Limasawa
Limasawa and Homonhon are the same place
All islands came under foreign rule at landfall
reason: For these selected stops, Homonhon came before Limasawa and Cebu. A visit is not proof of control.
definition: Reaching land after a journey by sea.

title: Homonhon: Help and Exchange
imageAlt: Local people provided food and drink; expedition members offered goods in return. A final card warns that help does not transfer authority.
content:
What did the newcomers need, and who could help? The NHCP Homonhon marker describes tired, sick and hungry expedition members. Local people brought food and drink, and the visitors gave goods in return. Local people took part in the encounter; they were not simply scenery around the ships.

Help and exchange can happen together. Providing food may help someone recover. Giving an object in return is an exchange. Neither action alone proves permanent friendship or agreement to foreign rule.

Try a fictional classroom comparison. One card says a visitor receives water. Another says the visitor hands over an object. You may describe help and exchange. You cannot invent a speech saying the helper gave away their home. These cards are learning prompts, not quotations from 1521.

For your report, name a supported action: local people provided supplies. Add a limit: this encounter does not tell us what every community thought.
clues: A need
The marker describes expedition members who needed food, drink and rest.
Local action
People from nearby islands provided supplies; expedition members offered goods in return.
What help does not prove
Giving food is not evidence that a community surrendered its authority.
task: What does the Homonhon supply exchange support?
Local people actively helped and exchanged goods with the expedition
The visitors found islands with no people or history
Giving supplies automatically surrendered local authority
Every later encounter must have been peaceful
reason: The supply exchange shows local action and assistance. It does not establish surrender or one response from all communities.
definition: Giving and receiving things between people.

title: Limasawa: Communication Matters
imageAlt: An interpreter helps a speaker and listener communicate. A separate event card names the recorded Easter Sunday Mass at Limasawa on 31 March 1521.
content:
An interpreter helps people communicate across languages. Accounts of the expedition describe Enrique serving as an interpreter. His language knowledge mattered, along with the knowledge of people he met. Sharing a language does not prove that everyone understood every idea in exactly the same way.

At Limasawa, the expedition met local leaders. The NHCP recognizes Limasawa as the site of the recorded Easter Sunday Mass on 31 March 1521. A Mass is a Catholic religious service. Students do not need to share a religious belief to learn about it respectfully.

Try a fictional worked example. A visitor asks for supplies through an interpreter. Before writing that an agreement was made, ask what was requested and what response was recorded. Hearing a request is not the same as accepting it.

Keep separate claims in your journal: communication helped people meet; a service was recorded. Neither shows that everyone across the islands adopted one faith.
clues: A communication role
Enrique helped interpret. A language skill is different from authority over the people speaking.
A named event
Limasawa is the NHCP-recognized site of the recorded Easter Sunday Mass on 31 March 1521.
Respect and limits
Studying a religious event does not require practising the religion. One event does not show everyone converted.
task: Which statement uses the Limasawa evidence carefully?
A Catholic service was recorded there; this does not establish conversion of every island
Everyone in the archipelago immediately adopted one faith
An interpreter could decide for all local leaders
Hearing a request always meant agreeing to it
reason: An interpreter helps communication. The recorded Limasawa service is a specific event, not evidence of universal conversion.
definition: A person who helps people speaking different languages understand each other.

title: Cebu: Leaders Make Choices
imageAlt: A report guide separates a recorded event, a possible explanation and a claim that still needs evidence. One group's decision is not everyone's decision.
content:
The expedition reached Cebu on 7 April 1521. The NHCP Cebu marker describes an active trading place led by Rajah Humabon. Trade and leadership already existed before the visitors arrived.

The marker records Christian baptisms on 14 April, including Humabon. Baptism is a Christian religious ceremony. Naming an event is different from knowing every participant's private reason. Religion, relationships and political interests can be part of an encounter, but we should not invent one reason for every person.

Check this report: statement A names a recorded baptism. Statement B says every community accepted foreign authority. A supports a specific event; it does not prove B. An agreement with one leader cannot be treated as the decision of all other leaders.

Local leaders made choices while other communities could choose differently. The next mission studies Lapulapu and Mactan. For now, explain the evidence about Cebu without treating the whole archipelago as one person's household.
clues: Before the visit
Cebu was already a trading place led by Humabon when the expedition arrived.
A dated event
The Cebu marker records baptisms on 14 April 1521.
Different decisions
One leader or group could not speak for every community in the archipelago.
task: What can a report about Cebu responsibly say?
Cebu already had trade and leadership, and the encounter involved local decisions
Magellan created Cebu trade from nothing
One leader could consent for every island
A baptism tells us every participant had the same motive
reason: Cebu had existing trade and leadership. Recorded choices there do not represent every person or every community.
definition: Leadership and decision-making within a community or place.

title: Check Who Tells the Story
imageAlt: A source check asks who made the account, what it describes, and whose views are missing. An account does not contain every person's viewpoint.
content:
How do we know about meetings long before photographs? Antonio Pigafetta travelled with the expedition and wrote an account. An eyewitness account comes from someone who saw or took part in events. It is valuable evidence, but a participant cannot see everything or know everyone's thoughts.

A modern historical marker is different. It presents a later summary based on historical work. It was not installed on the day of the encounter. Both kinds of source can help, but identify what each is.

Try this report task. A modern classroom card says a leader may have considered trade and safety. That is a possible explanation to investigate, not a recovered speech. Do not put quotation marks around invented dialogue and present it as the leader's exact words.

Ask: Who made the source? What does it describe? Whose view is absent? A visitor's account tells us what that visitor recorded. More evidence is needed before treating it as the thoughts of every person they met.
clues: A participant account
Pigafetta travelled with the expedition. His account records a participant viewpoint, not every local voice.
A later summary
An NHCP marker is a modern historical summary, not an object installed in 1521.
A classroom invention
A fictional prompt can help you think, but it is not an authentic historical quotation.
task: A classroom card invents a leader's speech. How should your report use it?
Identify it as a teaching prompt and seek evidence for historical claims
Quote it as the leader's exact recorded words
Assume it represents every community
Treat it as an eyewitness document from 1521
reason: Identify the source and its viewpoint. A fictional prompt is not an original speech, and one account does not contain all voices.
definition: A record by someone who saw or took part in an event.

title: Your Encounter Report
imageAlt: Report trail: Homonhon, Limasawa and Cebu. Selected events appear in order; the diagram does not claim control over the archipelago.
content:
Complete your encounter report. Start with a sequence: Homonhon, Limasawa and Cebu are distinct stops. Name an action: local people provided supplies at Homonhon. Explain communication: interpreters helped people speaking different languages meet. Name a setting: Cebu already had trade and leadership. Finally, identify a source and a limit.

Use this frame in your own words: At [place], [people] took part in [event]. The evidence supports [specific claim]. It does not establish [claim that goes too far]. This is a thinking tool, not a speech from the past.

Check your report. Did you confuse a landing with a sighting? Turn help into surrender? Treat a religious event as everyone's belief? Invent what a leader thought? Revise claims that exceed the clues.

The quiz asks five questions. If a topic is difficult, revisit its scene and use targeted practice before retrying. The mission reward is earned once. Chapter 5 remains unfinished: Mactan and later expeditions are next. This mission does not complete the chapter.
clues: Name the event
Keep the place, action and sequence together rather than listing names without meaning.
Explain participation
Local people helped, communicated and made decisions. Their societies existed before the expedition.
State a limit
A selected encounter and one account do not establish everyone's beliefs or acceptance of foreign rule.
task: Which report best connects the mission evidence?
The expedition met existing communities; encounters involved supplies, communication and local decisions
A landing immediately gave the visitors authority over all islands
Every person made the same decision at every stop
One invented speech explains every encounter
reason: A useful report connects specific events with local participation and states what the sources cannot prove.
definition: An explanation connected to evidence, with limits on what it can establish.
